title: Robust Identification of Drug Mechanism of Action Associated Genes Across Heterogeneous Drug Treated Datasets.

abstract: PD-1 inhibitors have revolutionized cancer treatment, but their antitumor efficacy is limited by various constraints, including the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME) driven by tumor-promoting tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs). Reprogramming TAMs toward an antitumor state is a promising strategy to boost PD-1 inhibitor efficacy. However, the strategies for driving this switch remain poorly defined. Herein, we identified N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase-V (GnT-V) as a critical regulator of TAM reprogramming and PD-1 inhibitor responsiveness. Single-cell transcriptomic analysis of PD-1 inhibitor-sensitive and resistant patients revealed that GnT-V expression was enriched in antitumor TAMs and positively correlated with the PD-1 inhibitor response. Validation data from spontaneous/xenograft tumors in mice and in vitro co-culture systems showed that GnT-V overexpression drives TAM repolarization toward an antitumor phenotype and enhances anti-PD-1 sensitivity. Mechanistically, GnT-V catalyzes β1,6-branched N-glycosylation of Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) at Asn526 and Asn575, stabilizing TLR4 and sustaining NF-κB activation to drive antitumor TAM polarization and T-cell-mediated antitumor immunity. To translate this mechanistic axis into a therapeutic strategy, we employed a clinically relevant mRNA-loaded lipid nanoparticle (LNP) platform for in situ TAM reprogramming. The mRNA-LNP platform delivered GnT-V mRNA with high stability, achieved efficient GnT-V expression in a TAM-preferential manner, and showed no apparent systemic toxicity. Functionally, the platform-delivered GnT-V repolarized TAMs, reshaped the immunosuppressive TME, and synergized with anti-PD-1 to improve antitumor efficacy in vivo. Our findings establish the GnT-V/TLR4 N-glycosylation axis as a switch that governs TAM reprogramming and offer a promising biomaterial-based strategy that combines GnT-V mRNA delivery with anti-PD-1 therapy to overcome PD-1 inhibitor resistance.

title: Reprogramming tumor-associated macrophages through TLR4 N-glycosylation: A GnT-V mRNA delivery strategy to improve PD-1 inhibitor responsiveness.

abstract: Adenoviral vectors have been widely validated as effective vaccine platforms for both infectious diseases and cancer due to their strong immunostimulatory properties. However, their application to personalized cancer vaccines and other time-sensitive antigens is limited by the prolonged production time required for conventional vector generation. Here, we developed an adenovirus-derived virus-like particle (Ad5VLP) platform that enables modular incorporation of antigen cargo without reconstruction of a complete antigen-encoding adenoviral genome. Ad5VLPs successfully packaged and delivered foreign mRNA, although mRNA-derived antigen expression remained insufficient to induce robust antigen-specific immunity in vivo. In contrast, direct encapsulation of protein or peptide antigens substantially improved intracellular antigen delivery and major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I antigen presentation. Following subcutaneous prime-boost immunization in mice, antigen-loaded Ad5VLPs induced robust antigen-specific interferon-γ (IFN-γ) responses, with functional activity preferentially enriched within CD44hi CD8+ T cells and accompanied by effector-associated CD8+ T-cell differentiation. Importantly, robust cellular immune responses were also observed using an E0771 tumor neoantigen, demonstrating that the platform extends beyond the model ovalbumin (OVA) antigen. Protein-loaded Ad5VLPs also elicited antigen-specific and antivector humoral responses. Vaccination was well tolerated over the 14 day study period, with no substantial changes in body weight, clinical observations, serum markers of hepatic or renal injury and systemic inflammation, or broad splenic inflammatory transcriptional signatures. Together, these findings demonstrate that Ad5VLPs enable modular delivery of protein and peptide antigens and induce robust cellular immune responses, supporting further investigation for personalized cancer vaccination and other time-sensitive vaccine applications.

description: JAR-2203 is an investigational small interfering RNA (siRNA) targeting LPA mRNA to reduce plasma lipoprotein(a) \[Lp(a)\] levels. This first-in-human, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study will evaluate the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics of single ascending doses of JAR-2203 in healthy participants with elevated Lp(a). Approximately 44 participants will be enrolled across six sequential dose cohorts, with dose escalation based on review by a Safety Review Committee.

abstract: Gene delivery is now a clinically established modality, but one of its central translational challenges remains: therapeutic performance emerges from a cascade of biological processes rather than from a single step. Lipid nanoparticles, polymeric carriers, and oligonucleotide conjugates undergo biological transformation, distribution and tissue access, cellular uptake, intracellular trafficking, endosomal escape, and ultimately functional payload delivery. The contribution of each process to the therapeutic outcome is context dependent and may shift with formulation, route of administration, target tissue, payload, and disease state. Consequently, transfection efficiency remains a necessary and widely used endpoint, but as a single aggregate readout it cannot by itself indicate which upstream process, biodistribution, uptake, trafficking, or endosomal escape, is rate-limiting for a given formulation, route, or tissue; resolving that bottleneck is the measurable attribute an in vitro-in vivo relationship must be built around. Classical in vitro-in vivo correlation (IVIVC) concepts were developed for simpler relationships, but their underlying principle remains relevant: identifying a measurable product attribute or process that governs in vivo performance. As pharmaceutical systems have become more complex, biopredictive methodologies have logically progressed toward process-resolved assays, systems-level understanding, and mechanistic modeling. Applying this principle to non-viral gene delivery does not imply that a validated IVIVC, or a regulatory biowaiver built on one, yet exists for these systems; rather, it asks whether the same underlying logic, identifying which step in a multi-step cascade is rate limiting and can be represented by a measurable in vitro assay, can be meaningfully extended from simpler dosage forms to a biologically complex delivery process. This review proposes a pathway toward IVIVC for non-viral gene delivery as a delivery cascade comprising three interconnected layers: (i) the Nanoparticle Biodistribution Layer, spanning circulation, biological transformation, and tissue access; (ii) the Cellular Delivery Dynamics Layer, encompassing cellular uptake, intracellular trafficking, and endosomal escape; and (iii) the Functional Therapeutic Action Layer, linking productive delivery to pharmacodynamic response. Each layer is matched with assays that isolate individual processes and expose where formulation performance becomes limiting. These layers have traditionally been studied by largely separate scientific communities, making their integration essential for understanding how performance gains or losses propagate through the delivery cascade. Rather than proposing a holistic IVIVC that does not yet exist for non-viral gene delivery, this framework provides a mechanistic roadmap for building it, moving formulation development from empirical screening toward stepwise biopredictive evidence and, ultimately, IVIVC for complex gene delivery systems.

abstract: A theophylline-binding RNA aptamer has been extensively studied as a model for RNA-ligand interactions. While previous structural analyses have provided insights into its binding mechanism, the precise nature of ligand recognition remains unclear. In this study, we present a crystal structure of a novel ligand-free conformation of the theophylline aptamer. Unlike previously reported ligand-free conformations within Fab-RNA complexes, the ligand-binding region adopts a well-organized structure in which the space occupied by theophylline in the ligand-bound state is instead filled by an RNA nucleotide. Structural evaluation with a residue-separation-based statistical potential revealed that the newly identified ligand-free conformation shows greater consistency with statistically preferred intramolecular atomic arrangements than the other ligand-bound and ligand-free conformations examined. These findings provide new insights into the conformational landscape underlying theophylline recognition.

abstract: Protozoan parasites possess complex genomes, unusual DNA-repair mechanisms, multiple developmental stages, and, in several species, intracellular or vector-dependent life cycles that complicate functional genetic studies. CRISPR-Cas9 has become a central tool for functional genomics in these organisms, enabling targeted gene disruption, replacement, tagging, nucleotide modification and genome-wide functional screening. However, editing efficiency and outcomes vary substantially among parasite species and depend not only on Cas9-mediated double-strand break formation but also on target accessibility, guide design, delivery method, parasite stage, DNA-repair capacity, donor availability, selection and the biological cost of the induced lesion. This review focuses primarily on experimentally established Cas9-mediated genome editing in Plasmodium, Leishmania, Toxoplasma gondii, Trypanosoma, Babesia, Theileria and Cryptosporidium. We compare plasmid-based and transient expression, ribonucleoprotein (RNP) delivery, electroporation/nucleofection, stage-specific delivery, guide and donor design, selection strategies, editing outcomes, and molecular and functional validation. Particular emphasis is placed on homology-directed repair (HDR), canonical non-homologous end joining (NHEJ), microhomology-mediated end joining (MMEJ) and single-strand annealing (SSA), which determine whether editing results in indels, precise sequence replacement, tagging or larger genomic deletions. Species-specific differences are illustrated by efficient NHEJ-mediated disruption in Toxoplasma, donor-dependent repair in Plasmodium and Cryptosporidium, SSA-associated repair in Leishmania, efficient homologous recombination in trypanosomatids, precise editing in Babesia, and stage-specific delivery constraints in Theileria. The review further examines the progression from single-gene editing to marker-free manipulation, base editing, conditional approaches and genome-wide functional screens. Cas12a, CRISPRi/a, prime editing and related systems are discussed as emerging extensions. Overall, this repair- and delivery-centred framework explains why CRISPR editing differs among protozoan parasites and identifies the experimentally validated limitations that currently shape their genome-engineering potential.

abstract:
MOTIVATION: The interaction between RNA and proteins is a complex process that involves atom-level details and dynamic changes. Accurate prediction of protein-RNA interactions helps researchers to develop protein-targeted small nucleic acid drugs. However, the scarcity of protein-RNA complexes and experimental data limits the ability of existing data-driven supervised learning methods to learn latent patterns, leading to limited performance.
RESULTS: In this study, we propose PRIDA (Protein-RNA Interaction prediction based on Domain-Adversarial learning), a protein-RNA interaction framework that combines bilinear attention with conditional domain-adversarial learning. Powered by pretrained protein and RNA language models, PRIDA improves interaction prediction under protein-level distribution shifts and limited labeled data. By integrating PRIDA with Monte Carlo Tree Search, we apply it to a virtual screening pipeline to generate RNA aptamer candidates for specific target proteins. Experimental results show that PRIDA achieves state-of-the-art performance in cross-domain protein-RNA interaction prediction and provides effective guidance for RNA aptamer virtual screening.
AVAILABILITY: The data and source code of the proposed method are available at GitHub (https://github.com/zhouyyang/PRIDA) and Zenodo (https://zenodo.org/records/23644677).
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

abstract: Lactobacillus johnsonii N6.2-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs) provide protection against murine norovirus (MNV-1) both in vitro and in vivo. Within the proteins enriched in EVs, the SH3b2 domain of Sdp was shown to be sufficient to recapitulate the antiviral effects shown by EVs. In this report, we compared the effects of six SH3b domains of Sdp and identified amino acids expected to be important for interactions with host proteins. We found that SH3b2 showed the highest activity in inducing NF-ĸB/AP-1 and IRF pathways in RAW macrophage reporter cell lines. Structure-guided site-directed mutagenesis of SH3b2 revealed residues in SH3b2 potentially responsible for interactions with host proteins. SH3b2-G501D had significantly lower stimulation of NF-ĸB/AP-1 and IRF pathways. In addition, SH3b2-G501D showed reduced IL10 and Oas1 mRNA levels, resulting in an impaired MNV-1 antiviral response in RAW 264.7 cells. mCherry fusions to SH3b2-G501D confirmed that the effects observed were not related to reduced uptake into macrophages, as quantified by confocal microscopy. Additionally, the role of the C-terminal linker sequence in Sh3b2, which is absent in SH3b6, in uptake or signaling in macrophages was evaluated. It was found that deletion of the C-terminal linker (SH3b2ΔC2 treatment) resulted in reduced promoter activity, while SH3b6::C2 partially regained function through restoration of uptake in macrophages. These results indicate that the C-terminal linker plays an important role in internalization by macrophages. We propose that once internalized, SH3b2 mimics eukaryotic SH3 domains involved in signal transduction to activate the cellular innate immune response in macrophages.

abstract:
The global objective of this Basket of Basket study is to evaluate the antitumor activity of each matched therapies that will be evaluated through the study in small molecularly selected populations.

The objective of module 1 wil be to determine the overall response rate (ORR) at 12 weeks by Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) 1.1 of atezolizumab in each of the arms of the module. All patients in genomically selected populations will receive atezolizumab 1200 mg IV every 3 weeks.

The objective of module 2 wil be to determine the overall response rate (ORR) at 16 weeks by Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) 1.1 of futibatinib in each of the arms of the module. All patients in genomically selected populations will receive will receive futibatinib, 20 mg, once daily (QD) in 28-day cycles.

The objective of module 3 wil be to determine the overall response rate (ORR) at 12 weeks by Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) 1.1 of amivantamab in each of the arms of the module. All patients in genomically selected populations will receive amivantamab 1050 mg intravenously (IV) for body weight \< 80 kg and 1400 mg for body weight \>= 80 kg mg once weekly in Cycle 1 (with a split dose on Days 1-2) and then every 2 weeks in subsequent cycles (28-day cycles).

description:
Basket studies are a new sort of clinical studies to identify patients with the same kind of mutations and treat them with the same drug, irrespective of their specific cancer type. In basket studies, depending on the mutation types, patients are classified into "baskets". Targeted therapies that block that mutation are then identified and assigned to baskets where patients are treated accordingly.

This protocol has two parts: part A (iPROFILER), which includes the common procedures for tumor molecular profiling and treatment recommendation, and part B (iBASKET), which corresponds to the therapeutic portion.

The purpose of part A (iPROFILER) of this study is to test participants' tumour tissue in order to identify whether their tumour has certain mutations in cancer-related genes. It is known that gene mutations of tumours contribute to their origin and growth and determine whether the tumour will respond to particular cancer drugs. This test will provide information about potential targeted therapies that specifically attack those gene mutations. The purpose of part B (iBASKET) of this study is to offer participants a personalised anti-cancer treatment based on the gene mutations that are found in their tumour.

Participants taking part in module 1 of part B (iBASKET) will receive atezolizumab 1200 mg IV every 3 weeks, following the analysis of their tumour in part A (iPROFILER). Participants will be able to take atezolizumab for as long as their tumour doesn't grow and for as long as they don't have any side-effects which prevent them from continuing treatment. Module 1 will have a 2-year recruitment period. The aim of the study is to determine which genomically selected populations respond effectively to the targeted treatment, atezolizumab. Approximately 1000 participants will be enrolled into part A (iPROFILER), with approximately 120 participants being recruited into module 1 of part B (iBASKET).

Participants taking part in module 2 of part B (iBASKET) will receive will receive futibatinib, 20 mg, once daily (QD) in 28-day cycles, following the analysis of their tumour in part A (iPROFILER). Participants will be able to take futibatinib for as long as their tumour doesn't grow and for as long as they don't have any side-effects which prevent them from continuing treatment. Module 2 will have a 2-year recruitment period. The aim of the study is to determine which genomically selected populations respond effectively to the targeted treatment, futibatinib. Approximately 1000 participants will be enrolled into part A (iPROFILER), with approximately 80 participants being recruited into module 2 of part B (iBASKET).

Participants taking part in module 3 of part B (iBASKET) will receive amivantamab 1050 mg IV for body weight \< 80 kg and 1400 mg for body weight \>= 80 kg mg once weekly in Cycle 1 (with a split dose on Days 1-2) and then every 2 weeks in subsequent cycles (28-day cycles), following the analysis of their tumour in part A (iPROFILER). Participants will be able to take amivantamab for as long as their tumour doesn't grow and for as long as they don't have any side-effects which prevent them from continuing treatment. Module 3 will have a 2.5-year recruitment period. The aim of the study is to determine which genomically selected populations respond effectively to the targeted treatment, amivantamab. Approximately 1725 participants will be enrolled into part A (iPROFILER), with approximately 69 participants being recruited into module 3 of part B (iBASKET).

description: The study population includes healthy adults aged above 18 years old who have received two doses of the Vaxevria vaccine, and are at least 91 days and less than 365 days after their second dose. Participants will be randomly assigned into two treatment arms. In each arm, volunteers will be randomized in a ratio Test vaccine:Comirnaty of 2:1. Each participant will receive one booster immunisation and will be followed for 6 months to evaluate immunogenicity response and assess the safety of the test vaccine in comparison to Comirnaty.

abstract: The purpose of this study is to determine whether carnosine (a food ingredient found in chicken and red meat) supplementation (2 g) for 6 months in participants with non-claudication and claudication peripheral arterial disease (PAD) improves walking ability. Previous studies with heart failure patients have shown that carnosine supplementation increases walking capacity in these patients.

description: The objective of this double-blinded longitudinal study is to determine whether carnosine supplementation (2 g) for 6 months in participants with non-claudication and claudication peripheral arterial disease (PAD) improves walking ability. In this pilot study we will enroll 144 participants that will be divided into placebo (n=60) and carnosine groups (n=60). We will measure the distance covered on the 6-minute walk test (6-MWT) and the pain free walking capacity on the treadmill before and after the placebo or carnosine supplementation. We will measure ankle branchial index (ABI) and blood flow by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) before and after the carnosine and placebo supplementation. In addition, we will measure carnosine by 1HMRS (Proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy), perform, global metabolomics and proteomics in the skeletal muscle, a comprehensive lipid and metabolic profile of blood, uptake of carnosine in red blood cells (RBCs), and measure carnosine aldehyde conjugates in the urine before and after 6 months of carnosine and placebo supplementation. Following completion of the study, we will follow the participants for another 3 months and examine the durability of carnosine supplementation.

abstract: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (AATD) caused by the PI⁎ZZ genotype (Glu342Lys) is characterized by hepatic accumulation of misfolded AAT-Z protein and reduced circulating AAT levels, leading to progressive liver disease and pulmonary emphysema. Gene correction therapy represents a potentially curative approach by directly correcting the underlying genetic defect. We report the first clinical case with direct assessment of hepatic gene correction by liver biopsy following in vivo base editing in a 66-year-old male patient with PI⁎ZZ AATD who underwent gene correction therapy within the YOLT-202 phase I/Ia clinical trial (ClinicalTrials.gov ID NCT07193615). Ten weeks after treatment, a liver biopsy was performed to assess hepatic histology in the context of pre-existing F2 fibrosis identified by elastography before treatment. Liver tissue was analyzed for correction of the PI⁎ZZ variant using Sanger and Illumina sequencing, including assessment of bystander and off-target editing. Serum levels and biological activity of AAT were assessed longitudinally using an elastase inhibition assay. Liver biopsy showed no evidence of hepatic inflammation and demonstrated correction of the PI⁎ZZ variant in 54% of alleles by Sanger and 57% by Illumina sequencing without detectable off-target signals. Following a transient post-treatment increase in transaminases, liver enzymes returned to baseline. Monthly measurements demonstrated sustained circulating AAT levels with preserved biological activity, as assessed by elastase inhibition, throughout follow-up. In vivo base editing achieved substantial and precise hepatic correction of the pathogenic SERPINA1 PI⁎ZZ variant, without concerning histological findings or detectable bystander or off-target editing. Sustained biologically active AAT levels support the feasibility and potential of this approach for the treatment of AATD.

abstract: Existing nucleoside analogues (NAs) and interferon therapy for chronic hepatitis B (CHB) have limitations, including drug resistance, low HBsAg clearance rates, and irreversible immunosuppression. Therapeutic vaccines, by activating virus-specific T cells and B cells, hold promise for achieving functional cure (HBsAg clearance + sustained HBV DNA negativity). This study is an open-label, single-arm, dose-escalation Phase I clinical trial. The study population consists of patients with chronic hepatitis B virus infection who have achieved virological stability following standard antiviral therapy. Phase I (dose exploration): three dose groups, with three patients per group. The primary objective is to observe and evaluate the safety of the WGc0201 vaccine in the study population (incidence and severity of adverse events).

institutions.label: West China Hospital

description: Although current antiviral treatments have achieved some clinical efficacy, there is still a lack of treatments that can truly cure hepatitis B, especially those that can completely eliminate HBsAg and prevent viral recurrence. Therapeutic hepatitis B vaccines are considered a potential treatment option for chronic hepatitis B and drug-resistant hepatitis B patients in the future. The development goal of therapeutic vaccines is to activate the body's specific immune response, promote the immune system to recognize and eliminate the hepatitis B virus, thereby achieving virological clearance and functional cure. WGc-0201 injection is an mRNA vaccine encoding the HBV-positive tumor antigen HBx. Preliminary basic research conducted by the team suggests that this vaccine has excellent safety, not only effectively clearing HBV DNA but also reducing HBsAg levels in serum and liver tissue while enhancing the expansion of specific T lymphocytes in the body. Therefore, we believe that the efficacy and safety of WGc0201 in treating hepatitis B warrant further investigation. We aim to use this Phase I study to preliminarily explore the therapeutic efficacy and safety of WGc0201 in this population and lay the groundwork for future clinical trials.

abstract:
This is an open-label, single-arm, dose-escalation study designed to evaluate the safety, tolerability, recommended subsequent dose, pharmacokinetic profile, and preliminary efficacy of JCXH-213 in adult patients with primary immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) who are refractory or relapsed after treatment with corticosteroids and second-line therapies.

The study consists of a screening period, treatment period, end-of-treatment visit, safety follow-up, and study withdrawal visit. Two dose groups are planned: 2 mg and 4 mg, with 2 patients to be enrolled in each dose group. During the treatment period, JCXH-213 at the assigned dose will be administered once every other day for a total of 7 doses. Assessments for safety and efficacy will be conducted according to the study schedule. After the last dose, patients will undergo an end-of-treatment visit and safety follow-up until the end of the study.

abstract:
UNLABELLED: Trypanosoma cruzi, the etiologic agent of Chagas disease, alternates between replicative epimastigotes and amastigotes and non-dividing, mammal-infective metacyclic and bloodstream trypomastigotes. Protein phosphorylation is a major regulatory mechanism in trypanosomatids, whose kinomes reveal an expanded family of NIMA-related kinases (NEKs). Here, we investigated the role of T. cruzi RDK2 (repressor of differentiation kinase 2), a conserved NEK that carries a C-terminal pleckstrin homology (PH) domain. Endogenous gene tagging showed that TcRDK2 is expressed in all major life cycle stages and displays a cytoplasmic distribution. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knockout of TcRDK2 did not markedly alter epimastigote growth in rich medium but caused a significant accumulation of cells with abnormal nucleus/kinetoplast configurations, consistent with defects in kinetoplast segregation and cytokinesis; TcRDK2-null parasites also showed reduced in vitro metacyclogenesis and failed to establish efficient infections in human fibroblasts. To probe gain-of-function effects, we generated tetracycline-inducible overexpression lines for full-length TcRDK2 (RDK2WT), a PH-deleted variant (RDK2ΔPH), and a catalytically dead mutant (RDK2K70A). Overexpression of RDK2WT or RDK2ΔPH decreased epimastigote growth, enhanced metacyclogenesis, and strongly impaired host cell invasion and intracellular amastigote proliferation, with more pronounced phenotypes for RDK2ΔPH, suggesting that the PH domain normally restrains TcRDK2 activity in vivo. Phosphoproteomic profiling of RDK2WT-overexpressing epimastigotes revealed broad phosphoproteome remodeling associated with TcRDK2 upregulation, including changes affecting proteins linked to translation initiation and the cytoskeleton. Together, these findings support a role for TcRDK2 as a NEK kinase in kinetoplast replication/segregation, metacyclogenesis, and host cell infection in T. cruzi and highlight TcRDK2 as a promising kinetoplastid-specific therapeutic target for Chagas disease.
IMPORTANCE: Chagas disease, caused by the parasite Trypanosoma cruzi, remains a major health problem with limited treatment options. To persist in both insect vectors and mammalian hosts, the parasite must precisely coordinate cell division, differentiation into infectious forms, and survival inside host cells. Protein kinases are central regulators of these processes and attractive drug targets, yet many remain poorly understood in T. cruzi. In this study, we investigate RDK2, a member of the NIMA-related kinase family. Using gene knockout, inducible overexpression, and global analysis of phosphorylated proteins, we show that RDK2 is required for accurate segregation of mitochondrial DNA, efficient formation of infective insect stage forms, and successful infection and replication in human cells. These findings identify RDK2 as a key regulator that links parasite cell division to infectivity and highlight it as a promising, parasite-specific candidate for future drug development against Chagas disease.

abstract:
UNLABELLED: Cervical cancer can progress from high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions driven by persistent human papillomavirus (HPV) infection. Identifying the gatekeepers restraining malignant transformation could reveal strategies to prevent and treat cervical cancer. In this study, we integrated single-cell transcriptomics, CRISPR-Cas9 screening, and organoid modeling to dissect this process. Single-cell analysis of patient samples revealed progressive activation of rat sarcoma virus (RAS) and proliferation programs along epithelial differentiation paths. A focused CRISPR screen in HPV-positive pretumoroids identified neurofibromin 1 (NF1) as the top suppressor of malignant transition. NF1 loss accelerated carcinogenesis in organoids, substantially shortening the experimental interval required for the emergence of malignant phenotypes and recapitulating basal cell expansion, altered differentiation marker expression, and tumorigenicity. Mechanistically, NF1 loss enhanced RAS-mitogen-activated protein kinase and phosphoinositide 3-kinase-protein kinase B signaling, promoted proliferative programs, and remodeled chromatin accessibility at regulatory regions enriched for activator protein 1 motifs. Conversely, NF1 restoration in cancer organoids induced apoptosis and suppressed malignant maintenance. Artificial intelligence-guided modeling was used to design a minimal NF1-derived peptide predicted to interact with RAS GTP-binding protein. The NF1-GAP-mimetic peptide reduced tumor organoid viability and cervical lesion-associated bioluminescence in an HPV16-driven mouse model and was associated with local immune-related changes without marked alterations in selected splenic T-cell populations. Together, these findings establish NF1 as a critical constraint on HPV-associated epithelial evolution and provide a time-compressed organoid model of cervical carcinogenesis, offering proof of concept for NF1-inspired therapeutic interception of RAS-associated signaling.
SIGNIFICANCE: Single-cell atlas and organoid screening identified NF1 loss as a driver of cervical carcinogenesis, which can be rescued with an AI-designed NF1 mimetic peptide that offers a therapeutic paradigm to intercept tumorigenesis.

abstract: Adoptive T-cell therapies using tumour-specific T-cell receptors (TCRs) are limited by competition with endogenous receptors, impairing efficacy and posing risks of off-target autoreactivity. Here we present a CRISPR-based platform that selectively eliminates both endogenous TCR-α and -β chains without affecting transgenic TCRs, irrespective of codon optimization. This approach achieves >90% deletion efficiency in Jurkat and primary human T cells, enhancing expression and functional potency of transgenic receptors. Using an HLA-A*02:01-restricted DMF5 TCR, we show that dual TCR ablation boosts antigen-specific activation and cytotoxicity in vitro and enhances tumor clearance in vivo in human immune system (HIS) mice and prevents graft-versus-host disease (GVHD). Targeted locus amplification showed that CRISPR-induced double-strand breaks did not alter lentiviral integration profiles, supporting genomic safety. Extending this approach to four insulin-reactive TCRs demonstrated that endogenous receptor removal increased transduction efficiency and functional activity, with one (1E6) showing selective activation and infiltration of islet grafts (SC-islets) in vivo. This study establishes a universal, safe, and scalable genome-editing platform for generating functionally precise human T cells. By integrating cancer immunotherapy and autoimmune disease modelling within a single framework, it provides a preclinical rationale for dual endogenous TCR removal to improve specificity, safety, and therapeutic efficacy in TCR-based cell therapies.

abstract: Polo-like kinase 1 (PLK1) is a highly conserved serine/threonine kinase that orchestrates key processes in mitotic progression, DNA damage repair, apoptosis, and immune signaling. Its frequent overexpression in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) correlates with tumor aggressiveness, poor prognosis, and resistance to therapy, highlighting its significance as both a biomarker and therapeutic target. This review systematically evaluates the molecular mechanisms by which PLK1 drives NSCLC pathogenesis, including its regulation by transcription factors, tumor suppressors, oncogenes, non-coding RNAs, and signaling pathways. We highlight PLK1's role in promoting cell cycle progression, chromosomal instability, metastasis, immune escape, and therapeutic resistance to chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and targeted agents. Furthermore, we summarize preclinical and clinical advances in PLK1-directed therapies, encompassing small-molecule inhibitors, RNA interference, gene editing, PROTACs, and nanomedicine-based strategies, with an emphasis on their potential to enhance sensitivity to existing treatments. Collectively, current evidence establishes PLK1 as a central hub in NSCLC biology and a promising candidate for precision oncology. Future investigations should prioritize biomarker-driven clinical trials, combinatorial strategies, and next-generation inhibitors for overcoming resistance and improving patient outcomes.

abstract: Base editors (BEs) are precision genome editing tools which allow for the efficient introduction of point mutations in live cells without using double-strand DNA breaks. The two main classes of BEs are cytosine base editors (CBEs) and adenine base editors (ABEs), which can introduce C•G to T•A and A•T to G•C mutations, respectively. Since their development, BEs have been further developed and improved to address issues related to efficiency, specificity, and precision. In this review, we briefly summarize several recent notable developments in the field relevant to their path to the clinic, as well as three clinical trials from the past three years which apply BEs to the treatment of T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, hypercholesterolemia, and a rare N = 1 urea cycle disorder. In these examples, base editing is used to precisely knock out genes or correct mutations back to wild-type in blood disorders and liver diseases. Through clinical trials, patients around the world are being treated with BE therapeutics, ushering in the next generation of precision medicine.
